sentence: [Electricians](/electrician-salary/) and [plumbers, pipefitters, and steamfitters](/plumbing-apprenticeship/) both fall under \"high school diploma or equivalent,\" the same label BLS uses for occupations with a few weeks of on-the-job training, even though a standard electrical or plumbing apprenticeship runs four to five years at roughly 2,000 paid hours a year.
target_quote:
coreSummary: 'The median annual wage for electricians was $63,190 in May 2025, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. The bottom 10% earned less than $42,640 while the top 10% earned more than $108,510. BLS projects 9% employment growth from 2025 to 2035, much faster than the roughly 3% average across all occupations, adding an estimated 75,900 jobs.',
'The Bureau of Labor Statistics tracks this role under SOC code 47-2111. For May 2025, BLS reported a median annual wage of $63,190, or $30.38 an hour. Separately, the employment-projection baseline counts about 821,000 jobs nationwide. The bottom 10% of earners made less than $42,640 a year, while the top 10% made more than $108,510, a difference of more than $65,000 between percentile boundaries. These figures do not isolate the effects of experience, licensing, employer type or region. BLS describes the job itself as physically demanding work, noting that electricians need enough strength to move components that can weigh up to 50 pounds and must be able to identify wires by color, on top of the troubleshooting skills the role requires day to day.',
'On growth, BLS projects 9% employment growth for electricians from 2025 to 2035, compared with 6% for construction trades workers as a whole and roughly 3% for all occupations combined. BLS classifies that as "much faster than average," one of the stronger outlooks among the skilled trades this site has covered so far.',
'BLS breaks out May 2025 wages by industry for electricians into four categories. Government employers, excluding state and local education and hospitals, paid the highest median at $79,820. Manufacturing followed at $74,550. Electrical contractors and other wiring installation contractors, the industry BLS says employs 66% of electricians (the largest single share by far), paid a median of $61,570, close to the occupation-wide figure. Employment services, which covers staffing agencies, paid the lowest of the four tracked categories at $57,760.',
'Per BLS, the typical entry-level education for electricians is a high school diploma or equivalent, with no postsecondary degree required to start training. Most electricians [learn the trade](/how-to-become-an-electrician/) through a 4- or 5-year apprenticeship, and BLS specifies that apprentices typically receive about 2,000 hours of paid on-the-job training per year of the program, alongside technical instruction covering electrical theory, blueprint reading, and code requirements. Some workers start out by attending a technical school first, which BLS notes can earn credit toward the apprenticeship, and workers with prior electrical experience in the military or construction may qualify for a shortened program based on testing. For the related power-line trade, see [how to become a lineman](/how-to-become-a-lineman/), which covers apprenticeship, CDL, and pay.',
"For readers comparing [entry paths that skip a bachelor's degree](/highest-paying-jobs-without-a-degree/), electricians sit at the higher-paying end of the occupations covered on this site so far. [Becoming a CNA](/how-to-become-a-cna/) describes a 75-hour federal training minimum for covered nursing-home work rather than a multi-year apprenticeship, and BLS puts the median nursing assistant wage at $42,260, well below the electrician median. [Medical assistants](/medical-assistant-salary/), whose typical entry credential BLS lists as a postsecondary nondegree award, unlike the apprenticeship electricians go through, have a median of $45,690. Electricians, despite requiring no postsecondary credential at all beyond a high school diploma, out-earn both at the median, though BLS does not track how apprenticeship length, licensing requirements, or industry mix account for that gap. [HVAC certification](/hvac-certification/), covering EPA 608 requirements, training, and pay, is another entry path this site covers.",
'BLS projects 9% employment growth for electricians from 2025 to 2035, adding an estimated 75,900 jobs (to a projected 896,900 total by 2035) and about 72,700 openings a year on average. As with most occupations BLS tracks, it attributes many of those annual openings to the need to replace workers who transfer to other occupations or leave the labor force entirely, such as to retire, rather than to newly created positions alone.',
answer: "BLS's most recent estimate, from May 2025, puts the typical electrician's pay at $63,190 annually, working out to $30.38 an hour. That figure splits the occupation exactly in half: as many electricians earned more as earned less.",
answer: 'Among the four industry categories BLS tracks for May 2025, public-sector work came out on top at a $79,820 median (this category leaves out state and local schools and hospitals, which BLS counts separately), with manufacturing next at $74,550, then firms that install and wire buildings at $61,570, then the staffing-agency category BLS calls "employment services" trailing the group at $57,760.',
answer: "Per the May 2025 data, the bottom-earning 10% of electricians made under $42,640 annually, and the top-earning 10% cleared $108,510, roughly a $66,000 spread between those two ends of the range. The Handbook doesn't say what specifically separates the highest earners from everyone else.",
answer: 'Most electricians spend 4 to 5 years training as an apprentice, per BLS, putting in about 2,000 paid on-the-job hours a year plus classroom coursework covering wiring theory, reading blueprints, math, and code compliance. Those who go through vocational schooling first often get apprenticeship credit for it, and people who already picked up hands-on wiring skills through military service or general construction work can sometimes test into a shorter track.',
answer: "Yes. Per BLS, the electrician workforce is on track to expand 9% over the 2025-2035 decade, well above the roughly 3% projected for the economy as a whole. The net increase is about 75,900 positions over the decade. Separately, the average of 72,700 annual openings includes growth and replacements, most of them opening up because someone left the occupation, not because a brand-new position was created.",
answer: "BLS doesn't spell out a formula, but its own figures show where six-figure pay tends to show up. The top-earning 10% of electricians already cleared $108,510 in May 2025. Government work paid best among the four tracked industries, at a $79,820 median. A related but separate occupation, elevator and escalator installation and repair, has a $106,580 median. An individual changing careers may earn a different amount; these national medians cannot predict that result.",
answer: "BLS treats \"electrician\" as a single occupation nationally and doesn't publish separate pay for specialties such as residential, industrial, or marine work: they all fall under the same SOC code, 47-2111. The closest official breakdown it does publish is by employer type, where the government-sector median outpaces manufacturing, contracting, and staffing-agency employers. Installing and maintaining elevators and escalators has a higher occupation-wide median, but it is a separate trade. The comparison does not measure an electrician specialty or the earnings from an individual career change.",

sentence: [Electricians](/electrician-salary/) and [plumbers, pipefitters, and steamfitters](/plumbing-apprenticeship/) both fall under \"high school diploma or equivalent,\" the same label BLS uses for occupations with a few weeks of on-the-job training, even though a standard electrical or plumbing apprenticeship runs four to five years at roughly 2,000 paid hours a year.
target_quote:
coreSummary: 'A plumbing apprenticeship typically runs 4 to 5 years, combining about 2,000 hours of paid on-the-job training per year with technical instruction in codes, blueprint reading, and math. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reports a median annual wage of $63,800 for plumbers, pipefitters, and steamfitters in May 2025, with the bottom 10% earning less than $44,150 and the top 10% earning more than $108,420.',
'Per the Bureau of Labor Statistics, most plumbers, pipefitters, and steamfitters learn the trade through a 4- or 5-year apprenticeship, though some attend a vocational-technical school first. Apprentices typically receive about 2,000 hours of paid on-the-job training each year of the program, alongside technical instruction covering safety, local plumbing codes and regulations, and blueprint reading. BLS also notes that apprentices study mathematics, applied physics, and chemistry as part of that classroom component. Apprenticeship programs are sponsored by unions, trade associations, and businesses, not run as a single national program, which is why the specific application process and waitlist can vary a great deal by local union hall or contractor. Most apprentices enter a program directly, though BLS notes some start out as helpers or complete a pre-apprenticeship training program in plumbing or another trade first. For a related trade, see this site\'s guide to [HVAC certification](/hvac-certification/), covering EPA 608 requirements, training, and pay.',
'BLS tracks plumbers, pipefitters, and steamfitters together under one SOC code, 47-2152, and one shared Occupational Outlook Handbook page; it does not publish three separate profiles, so every pay and employment figure on this page covers the combined group, not plumbers alone. The three job titles share the same core skills, connecting pipes and testing pressure so a system is airtight and watertight, but differ in setting and material. Plumbers install and repair water, gas, and other piping systems in homes, businesses, and factories, including fixtures such as bathtubs and toilets and appliances such as water heaters. Pipefitters and steamfitters, sometimes called fitters, install and maintain pipes that carry chemicals, acids, and gases, mostly in manufacturing, commercial, and industrial settings, with steamfitters specializing in systems built for high-pressure liquids or gases.',
'BLS states directly that apprentices earn less than fully trained plumbers, pipefitters, and steamfitters, and that their pay rises as they take on more responsibility during the program, but the Occupational Outlook Handbook page does not publish a separate apprentice wage figure distinct from the fully qualified median. The number BLS does publish is the occupation-wide median for May 2025, $63,800 a year, or $30.67 an hour. The lowest 10% earned less than $44,150, and the highest 10% earned more than $108,420, a spread of more than $64,000 that reflects where a given worker falls across the apprentice-to-master progression, license status, industry, and region, not any single factor.',
'BLS breaks out May 2025 wages by industry into four categories. Government employers, excluding state and local education and hospitals, paid the highest median at $71,660. Manufacturing followed at $65,770, ahead of heavy and civil engineering construction at $63,270. Plumbing, heating, and air-conditioning contractors, the industry that employs the largest share of workers in this occupation, paid the lowest of the four tracked categories, a median of $63,010.',
"BLS lists the typical entry-level education for this occupation as a high school diploma or equivalent, with no prior work experience required and on-the-job training delivered through an apprenticeship. After completing an apprenticeship and passing the required licensing exam, workers become journey-level plumbers, pipefitters, or steamfitters, qualified to perform tasks on their own, without direct supervision. Most states, and some localities, require plumbers to be licensed. Although the specifics vary by jurisdiction, BLS notes that states and localities often require 2 to 5 years of experience plus a passing score on an exam testing trade knowledge before allowing a plumber to work independently. BLS directs readers to their state's licensing board for the exact requirements and does not list every state's rules on its own page; this article follows the same approach, since a reader in one state cannot rely on another state's rules.",
"For readers comparing this apprenticeship route against other paths that skip a bachelor's degree, [electricians](/electrician-salary/) follow a similarly structured 4- or 5-year apprenticeship starting from the same high school diploma entry bar, and BLS puts their median annual wage at $63,190, within about $600 of the plumbing figure above. [Becoming a CNA](/how-to-become-a-cna/) sits at the other end of the training-length spectrum, a federal minimum of 75 hours rather than a multi-year apprenticeship, and BLS puts the median nursing assistant wage at $42,260, well below either trade. BLS data describes the aggregate labor market for each occupation; it is not a claim that any one of these paths is the better choice for a given person. Another apprenticeship trade, [becoming a lineman](/how-to-become-a-lineman/), is covered separately with its apprenticeship, CDL, and pay details.",
'BLS projects 7% employment growth for plumbers, pipefitters, and steamfitters from 2025 to 2035, which it classifies as much faster than the average for all occupations. That works out to an estimated 34,500 additional jobs and about 42,000 openings a year on average over the decade. As with most occupations BLS tracks, it attributes many of those annual openings to the need to replace workers who transfer to other occupations or leave the labor force entirely, such as to retire, rather than to newly created positions alone.',
answer: 'Most workers in this trade spend 4 to 5 years in a paid apprenticeship, receiving roughly 2,000 hours of on-the-job work each year alongside classroom coverage of safety rules, local code requirements, and how to read blueprints, according to BLS. Programs come through union halls, trade groups, and individual employers, not one standardized national curriculum.',
answer: 'Apprentice pay itself has no separate published BLS figure; the agency only notes that pay is lower during training and increases with added responsibility over the course of the program. What BLS does report is one combined figure for the trade: $63,800 a year ($30.67 an hour) as of May 2025.',
answer: "A candidate finishes an apprenticeship, then must pass an exam set by the licensing board in their state to reach journey level, which lets them take on jobs unsupervised. Requirements vary by state, but BLS says the typical bar is 2 to 5 years on the job combined with passing a trade-knowledge exam. A further exam, after additional years on the job, leads to master status in states that recognize that tier.",
answer: 'Yes. BLS expects this occupation to grow 7% between 2025 and 2035, well above the roughly 3% economy-wide average, adding roughly 34,500 jobs over the decade plus about 42,000 average annual openings. Most of those openings come from workers retiring or switching occupations, not newly created jobs. BLS separately flags rising demand for sprinklerfitters tied to fire-suppression building codes.',
